- Two basic methods: "COINAGE, or Coining, the art of making ma-ery, as performed either by the hammer or mill." (Inference: "ma-ery" is OCR-garbled; the entry frames coin-making as done by hammer or by mill.)
- Hammer method: blanks are cut from metal and each piece is weighed/filed to the standard weight; engravers prepare a pair of dies, one fixed in a block held "as any vice could have done" and one movable; a planchet is laid on the lower die, covered with the upper die, and struck "with a hammer ... till the double thamp was sufficiently ... impressed on each side of the planehet [planchet]." The finished coin must have the standard weight and mark "determined by the judgment of the ins[pectors], to make it good current money."
- Mill/roller method (modern): cast plates/laminae are passed repeatedly between rollers of a "laminating engine" rather than beaten on an anvil, giving "uniform and exact thickness"; round planchets are cut out with "a sharp ... trepan, of a round ... figure"; blanks are weighed, filed/forged to remove excess metal, "boiled and made clear" (annealed/cleaned), then struck between two dies "with one blow, forces the two surfaces or fields of the piece to fill exactly all the vacations of the two figures engraved hollow."
- Edge lettering: a machine with "two steel laminae," each engraved with half of the edge legend; a toothed wheel turns the planchet "so that it remains ... marked on the edge, when it has made one turn. Only crown and half-crown pieces can ... take the impression of letters on the thickness of their edges."
- A "coining engine or mill (fig. z.) ... may make many twenty thousand pieces in one day" for gold, silver, and copper planchets.
